before: throw signals a failure and transfers control toward a matching handler. Statements after the throwing operation inside that try block are skipped; a failed call does not supply its normal return value.

try encloses work that this boundary can handle. catch(const std::invalid_argument& error) handles that exception type without copying it. what() provides a descriptive string, not a machine-readable application protocol.

When stack unwinding occurs, destructors of fully constructed automatic objects in exited scopes run. Prefer RAII for cleanup. After this handler finishes normally, execution continues after the catch; an uncaught exception can terminate the program.

Expected output or behavior: reward 3

Optional local transfer task: Add a scoped object whose destructor logs cleanup, and trace its lifetime through the throwing call. You may trace this without a compiler; finishing the reading is not proof of a local run.
after: An exception signals a failure that interrupts the usual path. throw starts that interruption. A call that throws does not return its normal value, and the remaining statements on that path are skipped.
try marks the work covered by a handler. catch handles a matching exception type. const std::invalid_argument& reads this error without copying it, and what() provides its descriptive message.

Stack unwinding means leaving calls and scopes while an exception travels to a handler. Fully constructed local objects in those exited scopes are destroyed. RAII uses that cleanup to release owned resources.
The program prints reward 3, then after boundary on the next line. The score is allowed, so no exception is thrown and the handler is skipped.
If this handler catches a failure and finishes normally, execution continues after catch. It does not retry the failed call or return to the skipped output. An uncaught exception can end the program.
